analysis.one_liner: Blocked new offshore oil and gas drilling off North Carolina's Outer Banks until environmental studies were complete.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in two House committees and their subcommittees for the rest of the 101st Congress and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have prohibited the Interior Department from issuing new offshore oil and gas leases, approving exploration plans, or permitting drilling on the Outer Continental Shelf off North Carolina. The ban would stay in place until at least October 1991, and longer until the Interior Secretary certified — based on a new scientific review panel's advice — that enough was known about the ocean, ecology, and local economy to make an informed decision. It also directed new environmental studies, capped at $500,000, to fill those gaps.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal North Carolina communities and businesses. The bill's findings note that commercial and recreational fishing brings more than $1 billion a year to North Carolina and that tourism is the coast's largest industry, both of which could be disrupted by an oil spill or offshore industrial activity [S3]. Residents of the environmentally fragile Outer Banks would gain a guarantee that no drilling could be approved until the science was adequate [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: NC coastal fishing and tourism towns

how_it_helps.text: Bars the Interior Secretary from issuing new leases, approving exploration plans, or permitting drilling offshore North Carolina until the later of October 1, 1991 or a certification that environmental information is sufficient [S2][S3].

Requires new physical oceanographic, ecological, and socioeconomic studies and creates a five-member Environmental Sciences Review Panel to judge whether the information is adequate before the ban can lift [S2][S3].

The bill's findings cite the region's exceptional environmental fragility and the existing environmental reviews — from 1981 and 1983 lease sales and a 1989 draft report prepared with Mobil Oil — as insufficient and outdated [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil companies seeking to explore and drill off North Carolina — including Mobil Oil, which had signed a 1989 memorandum of understanding with the state and Interior over a draft environmental report [S3]. The Treasury would fund up to $500,000 in studies [S3], and if the studies eventually supported leasing, consumers could face delayed or forgone domestic energy production from that area.

drawbacks.text: The prohibition would block lease sales and drilling off North Carolina while studies were underway, delaying potential domestic oil and gas production and the federal revenue that comes with it [S2][S3].

The ban was temporary by design: it would lift by October 1, 1991 at the latest if the Secretary certified the science was adequate, so it deferred rather than permanently settled the question — and the scientific review could eventually clear the way for drilling [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the communities whose coast, fishing grounds, and beaches were at stake, the trade was modest: half a million dollars in studies and a delay in offshore energy activity, weighed against protecting a coast where fishing alone is worth over $1 billion a year and tourism is the largest industry [S3]. The bill was written to be a pause, not a permanent ban, which limits both its protective power and its economic cost. The main cost falls on a concentrated industry rather than the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 1990, sent to two House committees and then to their offshore-energy subcommittees, and no committee ever acted on it, so it died when the 101st Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Walter B. Jones of North Carolina introduced the Outer Banks Protection Act on January 23, 1990; it was referred jointly to the Interior and Insular Affairs and Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committees [S1][S5].
In February and March 1990 it was referred to the Panama Canal/Outer Continental Shelf subcommittee and the Water, Power and Offshore Energy Resources subcommittee [S5].
No hearings, markup, or floor vote followed; the final entry, on August 18, 1990, is a cross-reference to H.R.1465, and the bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil companies pursuing offshore leases off North Carolina were better off, since no prohibition was enacted; coastal fishing and tourism interests got no protection from this bill, whose substance the action history cross-references to H.R.1465 [S5].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore oil interests; coastal towns got no protection

for.name: Rep. Walter B. Jones
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; it received no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Interior and Insular Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 23, 1990 and referred it to a subcommittee; never reported it back or scheduled a markup.

against.name: House Committee on Merchant Marine and Fisheries
against.what_they_did: Received the bill jointly on January 23, 1990 and referred it to a subcommittee; never acted further on it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support or opposition never showed up in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have halted new leasing, exploration plan approvals, and drilling permits offshore North Carolina, directly blocking companies such as Mobil Oil, which had been working with the state and Interior on a draft environmental report for the area [S3]. Blocking drilling protects the coast's fishing and tourism economy from spill and industrialization risk [S3].

industries.industry: North Carolina commercial and recreational fishing
industries.note: The bill's findings put the fishing industry's annual economic benefit to North Carolina above $1 billion and flag it as vulnerable to offshore oil and gas development; the prohibition shields it until the science is adequate [S3].
Tourism is the major industry of coastal North Carolina, and the bill treats it as at risk of significant disruption from offshore development [S3].
